messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Tui was eight years old the night his world split apart. He had been playing in his room when he heard the first shout, then the crash of furniture, then his mother’s voice—pleading, then breaking. He crept to the top of the stairs and saw his father’s hand around her throat, the sharp smell of whiskey filling the hallway. Tui does not remember running down the stairs. He remembers the cold of the bicycle seat against his thighs, the way the streetlights blurred as he pedalled to the neighbour’s house, gasping. What he remembers most clearly is that he cannot remember—the minutes between the whiskey smell and the bicycle are a black hole, and when he tries to reach into it, his chest seizes and he feels the same terror, raw and unaged, as if he were still eight years old on that bike.

Now he is eighteen, a project manager at a small logistics firm, but the title feels like a costume. He manages a team of five, all men, and the mornings are the hardest. Every time he walks into the conference room alone with a male colleague, his skin prickles and he has to fight the urge to look for exits. He has taken to scheduling one-on-one meetings in open areas, or bringing his laptop to a coffee shop, because the closed door feels like a threat. He has stopped riding his bicycle altogether—the one he used to commute on—after the first time he climbed on and his hands went numb and he saw his mother’s face in the pavement cracks. Now he drives, even though traffic makes him late, because the bicycle is a piece of a memory he cannot trust.

His memory of that night comes in disconnected shards: the whiskey smell, the bicycle handlebars, his mother’s broken wristwatch on the floor, but never the face of his father, never the sound of the front door closing. The gaps terrify him more than the fragments. He is certain that if he could just remember the whole thing, he would know how to protect himself—but instead the terror arrives without warning, triggered by a clatter of a dropped pen or the thud of a car door. He jumps so hard at ordinary sounds that his colleagues have started to joke about his nerves. He laughs along, but inside he is scanning the room for a weapon, for an escape route, for the face of a man who might suddenly turn.

To quiet the vigilance, he smokes. He smokes on the balcony of his apartment, sometimes six cigarettes in an hour, because the act of inhaling and exhaling gives his hands something to do. He drinks most nights—just a few beers, enough to dull the edge of alertness, but sometimes more, sometimes until the fragments blur into something almost bearable. He has a girlfriend, Leilani, who has started to ask why he flinches when she touches his shoulder from behind. He tells her he is jumpy, but he stops meeting her eyes. What he does not tell her is that he watches every man who walks past their table at dinner, cataloguing their hands, their posture, whether they have been drinking. He does not tell her that he checks the locks on the apartment door three times before sleep, and once more after she falls asleep, because the click of the deadbolt is the only sound that quietens the watchfulness.

He came to therapy because Leilani gave him an ultimatum: talk to someone, or she could not keep living in the grip of a ghost she could not see. He came because the smoking made his chest ache and the drinking made the mornings worse. But what he said in the first session was quieter: he came because he is tired of living inside a war that ended ten years ago, yet every day feels like the moment before his father’s hand closed around his mother’s throat. He is afraid that if he stops watching, the violence will find him again. He is hoping, maybe, that the therapist can help him find the missing pieces of that night without breaking him in the process.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Avoid People: The vignette shows avoidance of specific triggers (men, bicycle) but does not depict avoiding other people generally. The patient works with a team, has a girlfriend, and attends therapy, indicating social contact is maintained.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

Tui was eight years old the night his world split apart. He had been playing in his room when he heard the first shout, then the crash of furniture, then his mother’s voice—pleading, then breaking. He crept to the top of the stairs and saw his father’s hand around her throat, the sharp smell of whiskey filling the hallway. Tui does not remember running down the stairs. He remembers the cold of the bicycle seat against his thighs, the way the streetlights blurred as he pedalled to the neighbour’s house, gasping. What he remembers most clearly is that he cannot remember—the minutes between the whiskey smell and the bicycle are a black hole, and when he tries to reach into it, his chest seizes and he feels the same terror, raw and unaged, as if he were still eight years old on that bike.

Now he is eighteen, a project manager at a small logistics firm, but the title feels like a costume. He manages a team of five, all men, and the mornings are the hardest. Every time he walks into the conference room alone with a male colleague, his skin prickles and he has to fight the urge to look for exits. He has taken to scheduling one-on-one meetings in open areas, or bringing his laptop to a coffee shop, because the closed door feels like a threat. He has stopped riding his bicycle altogether—the one he used to commute on—after the first time he climbed on and his hands went numb and he saw his mother’s face in the pavement cracks. Now he drives, even though traffic makes him late, because the bicycle is a piece of a memory he cannot trust. But the avoidance has crept wider. Tui used to have a small circle of friends from high school, but over the past year he has stopped answering their texts, turned down every invitation to hang out, and stopped going to his cousin’s barbecues. He tells himself he is just busy with work, but the truth is that being around any group of people—even people he has known for years—makes him feel like he is trapped in a room with no exits. He watches every face for a shift, every voice for a rise in volume, and the effort exhausts him. So he stays home, alone, where the only person he has to monitor is himself.

His memory of that night comes in disconnected shards: the whiskey smell, the bicycle handlebars, his mother’s broken wristwatch on the floor, but never the face of his father, never the sound of the front door closing. The gaps terrify him more than the fragments. He is certain that if he could just remember the whole thing, he would know how to protect himself—but instead the terror arrives without warning, triggered by a clatter of a dropped pen or the thud of a car door. He jumps so hard at ordinary sounds that his colleagues have started to joke about his nerves. He laughs along, but inside he is scanning the room for a weapon, for an escape route, for the face of a man who might suddenly turn. To quiet the vigilance, he smokes. He smokes on the balcony of his apartment, sometimes six cigarettes in an hour, because the act of inhaling and exhaling gives his hands something to do. He drinks most nights—just a few beers, enough to dull the edge of alertness, but sometimes more, sometimes until the fragments blur into something almost bearable.

He has a girlfriend, Leilani, who has started to ask why he flinches when she touches his shoulder from behind. He tells her he is jumpy, but he stops meeting her eyes. What he does not tell her is that he watches every man who walks past their table at dinner, cataloguing their hands, their posture, whether they have been drinking. He does not tell her that he checks the locks on the apartment door three times before sleep, and once more after she falls asleep, because the click of the deadbolt is the only sound that quietens the watchfulness. But he also does not tell her that he dreads her invitations to dinner with her friends. He has gone twice, and both times he spent the whole evening twisting a napkin in his lap, unable to follow the conversation, certain that someone at the table was about to blow up. After the second time, he made an excuse about a work deadline, and now he finds reasons to say no to every social plan she suggests. Leilani has started to ask if he even likes her friends, and he says yes, he just prefers quiet nights. She does not know that he prefers no nights with anyone but her, and even then he sometimes wakes at 3 a.m. and stares at the ceiling, listening for footsteps in the hallway.

He came to therapy because Leilani gave him an ultimatum: talk to someone, or she could not keep living in the grip of a ghost she could not see. He came because the smoking made his chest ache and the drinking made the mornings worse. But what he said in the first session was quieter: he came because he is tired of living inside a war that ended ten years ago, yet every day feels like the moment before his father’s hand closed around his mother’s throat. He is afraid that if he stops watching, the violence will find him again. He is hoping, maybe, that the therapist can help him find the missing pieces of that night without breaking him in the process. He is also afraid that if he lets people back in—if he goes to his cousin’s barbecue, if he sits at a table full of Leilani’s laughing friends—he will not be able to keep the terror locked behind his ribs, and everyone will see what he has been hiding all along.
